subject: math
label: Sequences & Series
blurb: Patterns that repeat by addition or multiplication — verified PYQs from JEE Main, JEE Advanced, BITSAT, and KCET, plus Cambridge IGCSE-style problems, graded by difficulty and tagged by technique. (Not tested on AP Calculus AB, which excludes series, so that board is absent here.)

toolkit.title: AP core formulas
toolkit.desc: nth term \(a_n=a+(n-1)d\). Sum of first \(n\) terms \(S_n=\dfrac n2\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]=\dfrac n2(a_1+a_n)\). Memorize both forms — the second is faster whenever you already know the last term.

toolkit.title: GP core formulas
toolkit.desc: nth term \(a_n=ar^{n-1}\). Finite sum \(S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}\;(r\neq1)\). Infinite sum \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\) only when \(|r|<1\) — always check this condition before using it.

toolkit.title: Three unknowns in AP — use a−d, a, a+d
toolkit.desc: When a problem gives three numbers in AP with a known sum, write them as \(a-d,\,a,\,a+d\) instead of three separate variables. Their sum is just \(3a\), which pins down \(a\) immediately.

toolkit.title: Three unknowns in GP — use a/r, a, ar
toolkit.desc: Similarly, three numbers in GP are best written \(\tfrac ar,\,a,\,ar\). Their product is always \(a^3\), which often hands you \(a\) in one line even before touching the sum or ratio conditions.

toolkit.title: AM ≥ GM for optimization
toolkit.desc: For positive reals, \(\dfrac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n}{n}\ge\sqrt[n]{x_1x_2\cdots x_n}\), with equality iff all terms are equal. Whenever a question fixes a sum and asks for a max product (or fixes a product and asks for a min sum), reach for this instead of calculus.

toolkit.title: Inserting means between two numbers
toolkit.desc: To insert \(n\) arithmetic means between \(a\) and \(b\): the whole run is an AP of \(n+2\) terms, so \(d=\dfrac{b-a}{n+1}\). To insert \(n\) geometric means: it's a GP of \(n+2\) terms, so \(r=\left(\dfrac ba\right)^{1/(n+1)}\).

toolkit.title: HP — take reciprocals to get an AP
toolkit.desc: A harmonic progression is nothing but a sequence whose reciprocals form an AP. Never manipulate HP terms directly — invert everything, solve the AP problem, then invert back at the end.

toolkit.title: aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁
toolkit.desc: If you're given a formula for the sum of the first \(n\) terms, the general term is always \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\) (with \(a_1=S_1\) as the base case). This works even when the sequence isn't a clean AP or GP.

toolkit.title: Telescoping via partial fractions
toolkit.desc: A sum like \(\displaystyle\sum\frac{1}{r(r+1)}\) or \(\displaystyle\sum\frac{1}{(2r-1)(2r+1)}\) is a disguised difference \(f(r)-f(r+1)\). Split into partial fractions first — almost everything cancels, leaving only the first and last pieces.

toolkit.title: Difference method for non-AP/GP sequences
toolkit.desc: If the differences between consecutive terms themselves form an AP (constant second difference), the general term is quadratic in \(n\). Build \(a_n\) by summing the differences, then sum \(a_n\) using standard closed forms — don't try to force-fit an AP or GP formula.

toolkit.title: Sum of first n naturals, squares, cubes
toolkit.desc: \(\displaystyle\sum r=\frac{n(n+1)}2,\ \sum r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6,\ \sum r^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2\). Recall these instantly rather than re-deriving — most "weird series" questions reduce to a combination of these three.

toolkit.title: Equidistant-term symmetry in an AP
toolkit.desc: In any AP, terms equidistant from the two ends sum to the same value: \(a_m+a_n=a_p+a_q\) whenever \(m+n=p+q\). This kills a lot of algebra in "find \(a_1+a_k+a_{2k-1}\)"-style problems — spot the index sum first.

toolkit.title: AGP — multiply by r and subtract
toolkit.desc: For an arithmetico-geometric series (an AP term times a GP term, e.g. \(1+3x+5x^2+7x^3+\cdots\)), multiply the whole sum by the GP's common ratio, subtract the shifted version from the original, and what's left is a plain GP you can sum directly.

toolkit.title: Exponential/log series as disguised AP or GP
toolkit.desc: A series like \(\log_{a^{1/2}}x+\log_{a^{1/3}}x+\cdots\) looks intimidating, but \(\log_{a^{1/k}}b=k\log_ab\) converts every term into a constant times an integer — the sum becomes \(\log_ax\) times a plain sum of integers.

toolkit.title: Product of GP terms via the middle term
toolkit.desc: For an odd number of consecutive GP terms, their product equals the middle term raised to that count: e.g. the product of 5 terms centered on \(ar^2\) is \((ar^2)^5\). Spotting this skips writing out every factor.

items: Three terms in AP: \(a-d,\ a,\ a+d\)
Three terms in GP: \(\dfrac ar,\ a,\ ar\)
HP: reciprocals of the terms form an AP
Product of \((2k+1)\) consecutive GP terms centered on \(ar^k\) is \((ar^k)^{2k+1}\)
